For an AHR test with a time-to-event endpoint, let
$\theta_k=-\log(\mathrm{AHR}_k)$, so that a positive value favors the
experimental arm. At analysis $k$, define the logrank score

$$
  U_k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} \Delta_i,
  \qquad \Delta_i = E_i-O_i,
$$

where $d_k$ is the total number of events, $O_i$ indicates that the
$i$-th event occurred in the experimental arm, and
$E_i=m_{i,1}/(m_{i,0}+m_{i,1})$ is its null expectation. The quantities
$m_{i,0}$ and $m_{i,1}$ are the numbers at risk immediately before the
$i$-th event in the control and experimental arms, respectively. Given
the risk sets, $O_i$ is Bernoulli with parameter $E_i$ under $H_0$.
Consequently, $\Delta_i$ has conditional mean 0 and variance
$V_i=E_i(1-E_i)$. Thus,

$$
  \operatorname{Var}(U_k\mid H_0,\text{risk sets})
  = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k}V_i.
$$

Let $\widehat\theta_k$ denote the AHR treatment-effect estimator. Statistical
information is the inverse variance of this estimator:

$$
  \begin{array}{c}
    ℐ_{k,H_0}=1/\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta_k\mid H_0),\\
    ℐ_{k,H_1}=1/\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta_k\mid H_1).
  \end{array}
$$

Under the usual score linearization,
$\widehat\theta_k\approx U_k/ℐ_{k,H_0}$ and
$ℐ_{k,H_0}\approx\operatorname{Var}(U_k\mid H_0)$. The null-standardized
test statistic is therefore

$$
  Z_k
  =\widehat\theta_k\sqrt{ℐ_{k,H_0}}
  \approx \frac{U_k}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U_k\mid H_0)}}.
$$

The null information fraction is

$$
  t_k = \frac{ℐ_{k,H_0}}{ℐ_{K,H_0}}
  \approx
  \frac{d_k/4}{d_K / 4}
  =
  d_k /d_K,
$$

where the event-count approximation assumes equal randomization. Define the
B-values on this null-information scale by

$$
  B_k
  =\sqrt{t_k}Z_k
  =\frac{ℐ_{k,H_0}\widehat\theta_k}
  {\sqrt{ℐ_{K,H_0}}}
  \approx \frac{U_k}{\sqrt{ℐ_{K,H_0}}}.
$$

As described in Section 2.1.3 of @proschan2006statistical, the stochastic
process formulation of @harrington1984procedures and @tsiatis1982group implies
that $(B_1,\ldots,B_K)$ behaves asymptotically like Brownian motion under
$H_0$. In particular, independent score increments imply, for $i\leq j$,

$$
  \operatorname{Cov}(U_i,U_j\mid H_0)
  =\operatorname{Var}(U_i\mid H_0)
  =ℐ_{i,H_0}.
$$

# Null hypothesis

The distribution of $\{B_k\}_{k = 1, \ldots, K}$ has the following structure:

- $B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_K$ have a multivariate normal distribution.
- $E(B_k \;|\; H_0) = 0$ for any $k = 1, \ldots, K$.
- $\text{Var}(B_k \;|\; H_0) = t_k$.
- $\text{Cov}(B_i, B_j \;|\; H_0) = t_i$ for any $1 \leq i \leq j \leq K$.

The derivation of the last 2 statement is

$$
  \begin{eqnarray}
  \text{Var}(B_k\;|\; H_0)
  & = &
  \frac{
    \text{Var}(\sum_{i=1}^{d_k} \Delta_i | H_0)
  }{
    \text{Var}(\sum_{i=1}^{d_K} \Delta_i | H_0)
  }
  =
  t_k\\
  \text{Cov}(B_i, B_j \;|\; H_0)
  & = &
  \frac{1}{\text{Var}(\sum_{s=1}^{d_K} \Delta_s\;|\; H_0)}
    \text{Var}
    \left(
      \sum_{s=1}^{d_i} \Delta_s\;|\; H_0
    \right)
  = t_i
  \end{eqnarray}
$$

Accordingly, $\{Z_k\}_{k = 1, \ldots, K}$ has the canonical joint distribution with the following properties:

- $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_K$ have a multivariate normal distribution.
- $E(Z_k \;|\; H_0) = 0$.
- $\text{Var}(Z_k \;|\; H_0) = 1$.
- $\text{Cov}(Z_i, Z_j \;|\; H_0) = \sqrt{t_i/t_j}$ for any $1 \leq i \leq j \leq K$.

# Alternative hypothesis

Under $H_1$, first define the statistic standardized by alternative-hypothesis
information,

$$
  Z_k^{(1)}=\widehat\theta_k\sqrt{ℐ_{k,H_1}}.
$$

The canonical joint-distribution approximation under $H_1$ gives
$\operatorname{Var}(Z_k^{(1)}\mid H_1)=1$ and

$$
  \operatorname{Cov}(Z_i^{(1)},Z_j^{(1)}\mid H_1)
  =\sqrt{\frac{ℐ_{i,H_1}}{ℐ_{j,H_1}}},
  \qquad i\leq j.
$$

Because
$Z_k=\sqrt{ℐ_{k,H_0}/ℐ_{k,H_1}}\,Z_k^{(1)}$,
the null-standardized $Z$-statistics have the following properties:

- $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_K$ have a multivariate normal distribution.
- $E(Z_k \;|\; H_1) = \theta_k \sqrt{ℐ_{k, H_0}}$ with the treatment effect as $\theta_k$ at the $k$-th analysis.
- $\text{Var}(Z_k \;|\; H_1) = ℐ_{k, H_0} / ℐ_{k, H_1}$.
- $\text{Cov}(Z_i, Z_j \;|\; H_1) = \sqrt{\frac{t_i}{t_j}} \frac{ℐ_{j, H_0}}{ℐ_{j, H_1}}$ for any $1 \leq i \leq j \leq K$.

The covariance follows from

$$
  \begin{eqnarray}
    \text{Cov}(Z_i, Z_j \;|\; H_1)
    & = &
    \sqrt{\frac{ℐ_{i,H_0}}{ℐ_{i,H_1}}}
    \sqrt{\frac{ℐ_{j,H_0}}{ℐ_{j,H_1}}}
    \operatorname{Cov}(Z_i^{(1)},Z_j^{(1)}\mid H_1)\\
    & = &
    \frac{\sqrt{ℐ_{i,H_0}ℐ_{j,H_0}}}
    {ℐ_{j,H_1}}\\
    & = &
    \sqrt{\frac{t_i}{t_j}}
    \frac{ℐ_{j,H_0}}{ℐ_{j,H_1}}.
  \end{eqnarray}
$$

The corresponding B-values satisfy

$$
  \begin{array}{rcl}
  E(B_k\mid H_1)
  &=&\theta_k\sqrt{t_kℐ_{k,H_0}}
  =\theta_k t_k\sqrt{ℐ_{K,H_0}},\\
  \operatorname{Var}(B_k\mid H_1)
  &=&t_kℐ_{k,H_0}/ℐ_{k,H_1},\\
  \operatorname{Cov}(B_i,B_j\mid H_1)
  &=&t_iℐ_{j,H_0}/ℐ_{j,H_1},\qquad i\leq j.
  \end{array}
$$

Thus, unless the ratio $ℐ_{k,H_0}/ℐ_{k,H_1}$ is constant
across analyses, the null-scaled B-values do not have independent increments
under $H_1$. Under a local alternative,
$ℐ_{k,H_0}/ℐ_{k,H_1}\approx1$, so
$\text{Cov}(Z_i,Z_j\mid H_1)\approx\sqrt{t_i/t_j}$ and
$\text{Cov}(B_i,B_j\mid H_1)\approx t_i$, recovering the canonical joint
distribution in Chapter 3 of @proschan2006statistical.

# Summary

|  | B-value | Z-score |
|:--------------------------------------|:---:| :---:|
|Expectation mean at the $k$-th analysis under $H_0$| 0 |   0 |
|Expectation mean at the $k$-th analysis under $H_1$| $\theta_k t_k \sqrt{ℐ_{K,H_0}}$ | $\theta_k \sqrt{ℐ_{k,H_0}}$ |
|Variance at the $k$-th analysis under $H_0$| $t_k$ | 1 |
|Variance at the $k$-th analysis under $H_1$| $t_k ℐ_{k, H_0} / ℐ_{k, H_1}$ | $ℐ_{k, H_0} / ℐ_{k, H_1}$ |
|Covariance between the $i$-th and $j$th analysis under $H_0$ ($i\leq j$) | $t_i$ | $\sqrt{t_i/t_j}$ |
|Covariance between the $i$-th and $j$th analysis under $H_1$ ($i\leq j$) | $t_i \; ℐ_{j,H_0}/ℐ_{j,H_1}$ | $\sqrt{t_i/t_j}\;ℐ_{j,H_0}/ℐ_{j,H_1}$ |
